newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: London coffee seen diving, El Nino a concern - trade.
newsitem.headline: London coffee seen diving, El Nino a concern - trade.

text.p: London robusta futures are tipped to plunge US$100-$200 later on Wednesday after New York arabicas tumbled overnight, Asian coffee dealers said.
"You can go $200 down on the numbers," one dealer said.

But other traders believe that $100 down is "more likely" and quickly point out that sentiment could easily do an about-face if any fresh weather forecasts emerge threatening the Brazilian coffee crop with frost.
"It (the London market) should be down by $100, but just as quickly as it fell, it can easily go back up again on any kind of Brazilian news," one trader said.

New York's July arabicas sank to a one-month low on Tuesday of 217.95 U.S. cents a lb in a frantic sell-off while London's July robusta contract shed early gains to end $65 down on the day at $1,825 a tonne.
"There's no more cold weather (in Brazil) for the moment. It's an opportunity to sell," a trader said.
"If we get the same thing, it could be bad. The Indonesian crop will suffer. The Vietnamese crop may also be hit if they get too much rain or typhoons."
The 1983 El Nino caused withering drought in Indonesia, the Philippines, Australia and South Africa while triggering severe flooding in India and South America.
Mor immediately, plunging coffee prices in New York and London have placed Indonesian coffee farmers and exporters in a dilemma, dealers said.
Coffee dealers said it was too early to be concerned over reports that a severe El Nino weather phenomenon is in the process of developing.

Meteorologists say the El Nino, a situation where abnormally warm water builds up off the coast of South America and can disrupt normal weather patterns worldwide, usually occurs once every three years.
But the last severe El Nino took place in 1983 and caused billions of dollars in damage to crops.
A veteran coffee trader in Singapore warned that if this El Nino is as severe as the one in 1983, there could be trouble.
When prices in London hit $2,600 a tonne two weeks ago, some Indonesian coffee producers held back in the belief that the price would eventually rocket up to as high as $4,000 a tonne.
"A lot of people in Indonesia were surprised. Two weeks ago, they could have sold their coffee at $2,300 (a tonne FOB Lampung). Today, it's below $1,600. That is a painful decision," one dealer said.
"Nobody wants to be the fool of the village and sell now. If there is frost in Brazil, prices could go up to $3,000 (a tonne) again," the trader said.
But another dealer said he did not believe prices would re-test recent 20-year highs when New York arabicas soared to a peak of 318.00 U.S. cents a lb.
"I think we've seen the highs for the year," he said, adding though that the direction of the market remains unpredictable. "The next thing you know, boom, the market can rally again."
Physical coffee business in Asia remained slow as people were glued to the sidelines waiting for New York and London to calm down.
"Nobody wants to do anything with the market behaving the way it is," one dealer said.

Trading in the robusta coffee contract in the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) reached 20 lots on Tuesday. Some 10 lots of the September contract were settled at $1,817 a tonne while 10 lots of the November contract closed at $1,814 a tonne.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
